author: A. K. Kaiza
title: Healing the Elephant: Life and History on the Mental Edge of Uganda
content:
Colonial governors live in the half shadows of history, and in Uganda the ghost of Sir John Hathorn Hall, in power from 1944 to 1952, repeatedly returns to mind – to think of the psychological wreck of the man under whose tenure Britain lost Uganda.




What did Hall think on that afternoon of 17 January 1952 when his plane flew him out for the last time? Would it have been far from what was going through President Milton Obote’s mind that dusky 27 July 1985 when he crossed the Kenyan border, or President Idi Amin’s during his helicopter escape from Kampala on 11 April 1979? Much graver would have been the minds of Kabaka Mwanga and Omukama Kabalega when the two monarchs were sent into exile in 1899. We can only imagine with horror the state of Kabaka Muteesa’s mind during that most fraught and dramatic exit in the country’s post-colonial history in May 1966.




The one constant of Ugandan politics is the brutality with which it dispatches its rulers.




The question rarely asked is what goes through the minds of the masses these men ruled over. For the crowd that thronged the capital on 10 May 1899 as Mwanga and Kabalega were marched into Fort Lugard on Kampala Hill, the disturbance dug deep. The Acting Commissioner, Lieutenant Colonel Trevor Ternant, may have expected a triumphant entry; after all, he was marching into the capital two men he had labelled as rebels. The scenes of despair and wailing forced him to quickly send the two away to Entebbe and organize a rapid evacuation to Seychelles. Here was tumult their world had not prepared them for, the caving in of the cosmos their heritage knew nothing else of life without, now facing a future no prior narrative had prepared them for. 




When it was over, and this future came, and they had lost their lands and freedom, the closure that came, first for Buganda in 1910 when at last Mwanga was buried, provided some solace; he had been dead seven years. For Bunyoro-Kitara, there was only heartbreak. The kingdom was buoyed first by the announcement that the old lion was on his way back. At the very banks of the River Nile, a place Kabalega named Mpumudde, I have rested; he died. Barely a kilometre from crossing the river. The final caving in of their universe was not helped by the salty funeral speech sitting governor Sir Geoffrey Archer gave at the Rukurato on his burial that April 1923. Bunyoro-Kitara’s world ended. The age would not extend to them the hand of kindness for generations to come. For the next twenty years, more than a quarter million died of sleeping sickness; the plague took thousands; forced labour, punitive taxation, and decades of enduring racial abuse followed.




What we now know as “psychology” came to our consciousness four decades after the burial of Omukama Kabalega. When psychiatrist Dr Benjamin Kagwa made a study in 1963-64, some revelation of what the common folk were going through showed. 




Glimpses of this disturbance we can catch when TikTok, Facebook, X, and Instagram revelations leave us stumped. They return in quotidian form what in bygone eras Ugandans framed in mythological terms. I recall with my child’s mind the air around 1979, at the fall of Idi Amin, rumours of a wooden-legged monster stalking the land; it was whispered that homes without a cross dug into the front yard would be visited by this creature. In Kampala, news spread by “Radio Katwe” – literally “head radio”. I do not recall anyone in Aboke digging crosses into their front yards. As it was with these whispered fears, what the calamity would be was never concretely stated. This was code-speak foretelling the fall of big men. 




Just before the fall of the Tito Okello regime, cassava and sorghum slurry brewing in vats, one for liquor, the other for beer, bubbled prophecies of end times. The man driving the Okellos to their fall, Mr Museveni, was called a changeling, able to turn himself into any creature or object when his pursuers came too close.




Such stirrings are beginning to disturb Uganda once again. Under trauma’s blind impress, the concrete and the quotidian recede into the realm of fantasy while myth congeals into fact.




Towards the end of 2025, the word “

gumite

” – loosely translatable as “toughen” – began to puncture speech. “Chwezi dynasty”, the second oldest of Ugandan myth tales, sprung a second-coming, and in the byways of town edges, where mechanics and fabricators, hawkers and layabouts hold court, the words “basement” and “fridge” are tossed about in jest. Be contrarian, argue stubbornly, and the threatening words, “You want to learn Runyankole,” provoke outbursts of Uganda’s disturbing morgue humour.




By the time he returned to Uganda in 1963, Dr Benjamin 

Kagwa

 had spent 35 years in the West, transiting through Europe to a medical degree in the USA. He left Uganda in 1928 to go study medicine, a young man the West took and, bar the two-year practice from 1963 to 1965, never returned to his ancestral land. But it is what he did in the 24 months he spent in Uganda, between 1963 and 1964, by which Dr Kagwa’s 44-year medical career is known. He is unknown outside the circles of specialist medical studies. He was a pioneering professional, one of the first African psychiatrists, a matter which would have meant little were it not for the study he carried out during his two years in Uganda and published as “

The Problem of Mass Hysteria in East Africa

”. 




Reports in January 1962 that girls in northern Tanganyika, in Kashasha, were laughing uncontrollably would not have made much sense, as they have barely done since. As described, the laughing episodes lasted hours. Authorities closed the school and sent the girls home. When the condition spread to where they went, with more girls and women beginning to laugh, it was described as a mass hysteria. It spread into Uganda. This was on the eve of political independence in East Africa; the timing lent readings of the event into the episode. Even decoding the mass hysteria in the less elevated genre of critique to call it a corporeal harbinger of end times takes some licence to live with.




Kagwa was born in 1903 to a high official of the Buganda Kingdom, the Mukwenda (chief of Singo County), Paulo Nsubuga Bakunga, one of the signatories of the infamous Anglo-Buganda Agreement of 1900. There was enough income in the families of beneficiaries of the land grab of 1900 for him to be sent off to Europe and North America for a medical degree, which he obtained in 1940 from the universities of Pennsylvania, Columbia, and New York. Makerere did not award degrees until the 1950s. As a qualified doctor and psychiatrist, there was the early drama of his fight with the British colonial government that warned him that if he returned to Uganda, he would only be granted African Assistant Medical Officer status. Kagwa chose to remain in the US where he set up a successful practice working chiefly with traumatized American war veterans. It was the independent Ugandan government that invited him back in 1963. He landed amidst the laughing hysteria and it was his analysis of it, grounding the phenomenon against the backdrop of the colonial and the decolonizing experience, that ensured his career some measure of posterity. 




“Mass madness” as a subject was not new. In the forms of the “running mania” that afflicted the eastern province of Bugisu in that era, of victims running till they collapsed, and of the Tanganyika “laughing epidemic”, the times provided direct interpretations. Kagwa 

theorized

 that these were “conversion reactions” manifesting physically; of the mental conflict brought about by the rapid drawing down of colonialism; of people caught between a traditional society and Western, colonial values. These physical manifestations, he explained, were not unique, but occurred wherever deep cultural foundations were violently shifted; the St. John’s Dance mania of 14

th

 and 17

th

 century Europe; French meowing nuns of the same period, and more recently in 2011, the New York Le Roy twitching outbreak that afflicted high school cheerleaders. Many explanations are given for these strange events – the black death, famine, and war in Europe, social media echo chambers (New York). Kagwa’s deductions were not an outlier. As for his career, Kagwa left Uganda in 1964 and returned to New York, where he died in 1984.




By 1964, when Kagwa’s study was published, Kampala and Uganda had been through the tumultuous, transformative 1950s, enduring the boycotts and anti-colonial movements of that decade. It is the second half of the 1940s that ought to concentrate our attention, the immediate events when the deep cultural foundations of colonial oppression were shaken. And so Hathorn Hall.




It is hard to get a proper handle on the careers of colonial governors. They attract less blame than post-colonial presidents even when post-colonial Africa is still grappling with the mess they created. The system they represented is long dead, so reckoning them into current political systems is unhelpful. Peculiarities now of the age of empire, colonial governors lie quietly in the sediments of dead city-states and sunken empire-states. They might come alive frequently, but in the same way that well-preserved fossils can be said to be lifelike. For practical purposes, they are the remains of a bureaucratic system whose evolutionary body plans the extinction of state systems constantly grind into history. 




In their time, they were commanders-in-chief, with the powers to commute sentences; they were not heads of state, which is why they lived in Government House; “State House” was Buckingham Palace. They had the privilege of honour, fawned upon in the territories they governed; they answered to the Colonial Secretary back in London – to a minister. They read budgets and opened Legislative Councils; their decisions could be easily revised by the Colonial Secretary. The answer to this paradox lies in how the British Empire reflected the core schizophrenia of its imperial personality. 




Democratically governed at home, the Empire needed a complex set of levers and pressure plates to transmit democratic power into tyranny without knocking out the administrative engine. Hence, along the drive train transmitting British governance of checks and balances into the racist, and not infrequently, genocidal policy overseas where the rubber met the road, a series of gears was developed: agreements with native potentates to make it seem legal; missionary education and hospitals to give it the gleam of civilization; imperial spectacle of Empire Day, Jubilees, 

sports

, and the King’s African Rifles band as a veneer of joy. Underneath all these, the business of forced labour and punitive taxation kept the real intent burning.




The contradictions were built-in, unintended obsolescence design that frequently jammed the imperial motor. How was it that a man appointed governor, with all the powers and status that the position conferred, driving with the ensign of office, be junior in reporting rank to a cabinet minister and be supervised by an undersecretary who might commute on the underground? The imperial vintage sputtered and broke down when external overload from the world wars overwhelmed its tonnage limit.




This explanation sets in perspective the response to the double crises that befell Hall’s tenure, first in 1945 and then 1949, not unlike the tragic engineering by which an elected president now attempts to cede power to an unelected son.




Nothing on the scale of the 1945 strikes and the 1949 riots had destabilized the colonial administration since the 1897 mutiny. It was ready-made karma. The mercenary army of Sudanese soldiers forced to suppress fellow Muslims in Buganda turned against the British. Until 1945, the administration had long disregarded African complaints about taxation, forced labour, underpayments for cash crops, and racial discrimination. The colonial framework that denied black people agency blinded the administration to what came next. 




Hathorn Hall was away on tour in Karamoja on 16 January 1945 when he received a message urgently urging him back to Entebbe. He had come to Uganda to replace the feckless Sir Charles Dundas, 8

th

 governor to Uganda, on 19 December 1944, and was barely a month into the job. 




The strike began when “houseboys” and “housegirls” in Entebbe walked out. Frozen wages – £1 a month – amidst the rising cost of living, long, unregulated work hours, and atrocious housing on the “septic fringe” slums were their conditions. They were quickly joined by drivers in Kampala and Jinja, before other sectors joined in. In its January 17 edition, the settlers’ mouthpiece, 

The Uganda Herald

, running to 28 pages at the time, could only print 337 words after its typesetters walked out in solidarity.




Wartime import controls collapsed supplies. Maize and wheat flour, soap, medicine, and even matchboxes were hard to find. Failed rains in 1942 occasioned famine in Uganda, and although the rains returned in 1943, the impact continued long into the following year. The war did not directly touch Uganda, but as Governor Mitchell had urged, the country could fight it by contributing cash to the war effort. From 1940, the War Funds drove a nationwide campaign to raise money. Stuttering at the beginning, it gained traction with better marketing. Uganda was urged to raise money to fund a fighter squadron. The target sum of £100,000 was met and sent to England; the Royal Air Force bought aircraft and created the Uganda Squadron. This was early in the war. As it dragged on, there were other marketing gimmicks, including money for 

H.M.S. Uganda

, a warship. There were other demands for donations: the Bombed Babies Fund, Polish Refugee Funds, Air Raid Victims Fund, Netherlands Relief Fund; there were nearly twenty causes the colony was asked to give money for.




The War Funds drive was the first mass-participation event that created the first consciousness of “Uganda”: names of commoners, their counties and villages were listed alongside the sums they had contributed. Asians contributed handsomely as did the European population. It was a draining experience driven by a coercive publicity machine at a time of reduced incomes.




Rationing was introduced. The order was not given openly. But it has long been the view among Ugandan historians that it was an open secret that the colonial administration instructed shops and bakeries to prioritize Europeans and Asians. When Africans turned up, they were told there was no bread. They could not buy soap, medicine, or matchboxes. As they watched, Europeans and Asians waltzed in, bought what the Africans were told was unavailable, and then walked out. For the domestic servants, seeing these very items they could not buy in the very houses they cleaned was asking too much. This episode only served to sour an already bad relationship between Africans and Indians, for it was they who ran the shops and bakeries, and owned the cinemas that practised segregation.




For a while, in the early years of the war, the racial segregation that had seen Africans stopped at cinema box offices and told there were no more tickets available for sale, only for Europeans and Asians to walk in and buy the same, had seemed past. In the months when the Battle of Britain intensified, Africans were allowed into cinemas even on days when the showing had been only for Europeans. Even more, African music and dances were permitted inside the cinema theatres, and once, even the Buganda Anthem, 

Twesimye Nnyo

, was permitted performance within the White and Asian-only zone of Kampala. But, as even Africans understood, the colour bar was lowered only so they could perform and sell tickets for the War Funds. The tide of the war against the Axis powers turned, and these racial rapprochements were abandoned.




In confirmation that the colonial economy depended on half-free African labour, Asian and European businesses shut down once the strikes took hold. Limited transportation for the nascent Uganda Transport Company (UTC), operating since 1939, was only possible after Asian drivers were called in. Telegraph lines were severed. Milk supplies ceased. In Kisoga, the junction town south of Mukono town, strike enforcers tipped milk cans from the Polish refugee camp in Koja into the ground. Meat and vegetable supplies into Kampala were relieved by train transportation from Kenya. In a further poisoning of relations with Africans, gangs of volunteer Asian strike breakers, encouraged by the administration, drove in trucks arresting and beating up strikers.




When it was over, and eight Africans had been shot dead, Sir Hathorn Hall made nary a mention of the economic hardship and discrimination, nor did he make attempts to explain why Africans who had emptied their pockets for the War Funds were denied bread. All the while, the Uganda Squadron, renamed from Squadron No. 46, fitted with Hawker Hurricanes, was winning spectacular battles against the axis powers. The matter was political, he insisted, explaining that meetings had been held and plans laid out to sabotage the protectorate. And although a backhanded acknowledgement was made via a published schedule for raising African incomes, Africans who turned up at Asian shops continued to find they could not buy bread. When wheat supplies eased, they were only sold brown bread; African bread. Not the white loaves.




Hathorn Hall was arguably the first governor forced into open policy deception. He had to adopt double speak to acknowledge African contributions to the war (77,000 Ugandans were drafted) while laundering social and economic injustices into political accusations. The real damage from the strikes was the collapse of the racial hierarchy the African strikers breached.




As the years swept into 1949, accusations against agitators mirrored the times. Since the 1930s, Ignatius (an apt name for a man who sparked off political consciousness) Kangave Musaazi and the Bataka land grievance movement of Buganda had steadily rewritten the colonial script. This script had stated that Africans were bereft of political imagination. If they had no brains to think with, how could they by themselves organize a strike? It had to be the Bolsheviks. A different language by which to imagine the African world was urgently needed. Before the embers of the strike had cooled, another explanation was quickly called for on 5 September 1945, when the Buganda Katikiro, Martin Luther Nsibirwa, was shot dead on the steps of Namirembe Cathedral. 




Here was a situation where the truth could not so easily be bent by rhetoric. This was a long-coming riposte to the 1900 land grab. Not since 1888, when the magnificent Katikiro, Mukasa, was killed, had commoners turned against a Mengo potentate. This was Nsibirwa’s second stint in power. He had been Katikiro throughout the 1930s, resigning in 1940 when the Bakaka pressure against Mengo (land, taxation, and nepotism) would not allow him to remain in power. He was returned after the strikes by the British, as a man with the wiles and the force to face down the agitators. He was well appointed, and in this choice, Hathorn Hall was digging in. Nsibirwa had been a protege of Sir Apollo Kagwa. Kagwa had been prime minister, or Katikiro, of Buganda from 1888 to 1936, an absolute ruler who presided over the massive mailo land grabs and oversaw forced labour upon his own people. As a young man, Nsibirwa grew up under the tutelage of Kagwa and had watched the signing of the 1900 Agreement. For the Buganda commoner, Nsibirwa epitomized land injustice. But the casus belli was more immediate, albeit in the same fashion. Nsibirwa had forced through the giveaway of Mulago and Makerere to the British, a matter that the segregated Kampala Township had long wanted but which Buganda resisted. It was for this direct reason that George William Senkatuka shot him.




Some realization that what was happening was for real would have begun to dawn upon Hathorn Hall after this. But the moment never arrived when they would acknowledge the black man’s agency. Like King Lear, Hathorn slipped into fantasy. He began to see Bolsheviks everywhere. The inclusion of African representatives to the Legislative Council, 25 years since it first sat in 1921, only added insult to African injury. The men chosen, including Nsibirwa’s successor, Michael Kawalya-Kagwa as Katikiro, inflamed feelings even more, for he was the son of the hated Apollo Kagwa himself. If Hathorn Hall had dug in with the reappointment of Nsibirwa, in appointing Kawalya-Kagwa, he was firing a ballistic missile into the affray.




Although intelligence forewarned the administration of trouble coming in 1949, it was the scale and virulence of it, along with the Shakespearean phantasm about those fictional, brainless black men that blinded them to the flesh-and-blood Africans living all around them that caught the administration off guard. Colonial policy had been designed for the governance of Africans who existed only in their imagination.




Kabaka Edward Muteesa was the first to publicly announce, on 24 April 1949, that trouble was coming. Amidst the demands that they be allowed to gin their own cotton against the entrenched interests of Asian and European ginners, the Bataka movement made demands which may have been fashioned to result in denial; to demand that the Kabaka sack his three ministers (including Kawalya-Kagwa, whose replacement needed the governor’s approval) and county chiefs who had declared the Bataka an illegal movement was a high-stakes move. The Kabaka told them he would consider it. Three hours later, he said he would not. 




The dispersal of agitators that day gave Kampala a false sense of hope that trouble was averted. It was in the morning, on 26 April, that the reading of the Riot Act by Kampala Assistant Resident J.V. Wild ended abruptly when a piece of wood was thrown at him. He was taken to hospital. The baton charge dispersed the crowd. In the Mengo area, groups of people hurled stones at passing cars. The house of the Omuwanika – treasurer and one of the three ministers the movement wanted sacked – was attacked and an attempt was made at the residence of the Omulamuzi – the justice minister.




It had begun. The rapidity with which the rioting spread – for it was not a strike – was breathtaking. First Kampala was declared a disturbed area. The next day, all of Buganda was declared a disturbed area. The targets of the riots sketched the trail of political feelings. Rioters drove long distances just to burn down the houses of particularly hated county chiefs. A gang went out in Kampala to burn down the house of the Kabaka’s personal purser. In total, 400 properties were burned down. Indian shops were looted. Ginneries were so central to the lucrative cotton trade that special security was organized to safeguard them. More than a thousand individuals were prosecuted. Fourteen prominent Baganda leaders, including a clergyman, were deported on accusations of belonging to the Bataka movement.




Hathorn Hall was presiding over a fast-sinking imperial prestige. Here was the empire stumbling through African villages begging for money to defend the independence of Great Britain; only the fantasy African inside their heads could not read this irony. The withdrawal, then reinstatement of racial discrimination in Uganda’s towns for the sake of raising money was the mask slipping he could not convincingly put back on. After 1949, commitments to grant Africans ginning rights, and the six-year economic plan for industrialization cratered the very foundations of this prestige. After him, Governor Andrew Cohen’s governing could only be as management of imperial decline. Strange things began to happen. Racial lines were crossed; Africans of high standing were invited into clubs once barred to them (in April 1945, a surreal event occurred in Kampala when the Goan Institute held an “All Race Dance” and invited a handful of Africans, including a young Godfrey Binaisa for a send-off party to their university studies in England; Africans had previously attended these events to serve drinks). But the damage had been done, and the general boycott of Asian and European businesses when it came in the late 1950s trampled over the late-stage imperial attempts at redress.




Did Dr Kagwa (no relation to Apollo) catch the mental strains navigating these tumults inflicted on Ugandans?




Shifting post-colonial mental gears 




The switch from colonialism to independence did not cure the country of colonialism. It changed the 

dramatis personae

. If the killing of Nsibirwa had been any indication, now a war was beginning between colonial collaborators and nationalists. The break between the central government and the Buganda Kingdom in 1966 has been much written about, including psychological studies about the impact that the attack on the Lubiri had on Buganda – or sections of Buganda that did not include followers of the Bataka movement. The referendum over the so-called lost counties of Bunyoro-Kitara, which the British granted Buganda in payment for their help in subduing Kabalega, had lain as an unexploded political ordinance. A colonial-era commission had pronounced itself on the matter and organized the referendum, which, by an overwhelming majority, voted for the removal of Banyoro land from Buganda ownership. Prime Minister at the time, Milton Obote, made good on this result. Kabaka Muteesa’s response was to order Obote to remove his government from Buganda soil.




Era by era, the history of Uganda is a history of trauma. You learn as much by scouring psychology papers as you learn by reading Prof. Mahmood Mamdani. Since the 1970s, “war trauma” has characterized psychological research in Uganda. Beginning in the 1970s, scholars started to see Uganda as a “theatre of terror”, driven by the “cult of personality”, in which public executions, poverty, ethnic cleansing, scapegoating of Ugandan Asians and displacement came to be normalized. President Idi Amin’s era was the birth of the “big man”, the infallible man who ruled by decree. This quietened down after his fall. Uganda now is on the verge of a return to the era of the big man and rule by decree.




After the 1972 expulsion of Asians, Uganda’s conflicts took a radical shift. Ugandan refugees became the unenviable first cohort to undergo studies of trauma and displacement. Barbara Harrel-Bond, in her 1982 paper, “Ugandan Refugees in the Sudan”, flagged post-traumatic stress disorders (PTSD) and depressive disorders among the refugees from the witnessing of families beaten and executed, added to what she described as “refugee precarity” – the loss of social safety nets, poverty, food scarcity, and displacement. Later studies discovered that parents passed on these conditions to their children – PTSD as a family heirloom. Bert Adams, of the University of Wisconsin and teaching at Makerere in 1972, in the paper, “Ugandan Asian Expulsion Experiences: Rumour and Reality”, diagnosed suppressed trauma among Ugandan Asians living in the diaspora many years after the expulsion and despite leading successful lives in the West.




A country of unrelenting cruelty. The northern war of 20-plus years has generated the most papers. Ocaka, Browne et al., writing in 

BioMed Central

, reported that a staggering 54 per cent of northern Ugandans were suffering from PTSD while the even more alarming figure of 67 per cent presented “major depression”. These figures were even higher among formerly abducted children. Schauer, E. & Elbert, T., publishing in 

VIVO

, the paper, “

The psychological impact of war and displacement on children in Northern Uganda

”, said that returnees coming home suffered trauma triggers from scenes at home where they had been abducted.




In the paper, “

Cango Lyec (Healing the Elephant): HIV Incidence in Post-Conflict Northern Uganda

”, Achilles Kiwanuka and a team of researchers detailed what its authors termed the long tail of trauma: that prolonged trauma seeped into life-long term, with sufferers also most likely to have unstable marriages and to show reduced HIV/AIDS immunity.




These are major studies of extremes. In my own study of urban culture, I encountered the ingraining of this history in settlement patterns, of slums in Kampala patterning out the many stages of traumatic pasts – older slums closer to the city centre, Kamwokya-Kyebando, Kagugube tended to host third-generation victims of the wars and the HIV/AIDS pandemic of the 1980s. Newer slums of eastern Kampala were home to victims of the northern and eastern Uganda wars of the 1990s and early 2000s. 




Modern Ugandan public culture is shaped by these histories. The Ugandan 

“bifunda”,

 the roadside bar, a social institution, was itself a product of the civil war era when formal bars too far from home were a danger; trauma as a deconstructor of urban physical planning. The traditional music of Buganda and of northern Uganda is a repository of what the psychologists describe, so much so that “trauma music” may be a genre unto itself. Kandongo Kamu music of the late 1950s and early 1970s casually describes coming to Kampala as a black man and woman.




The new reign of terror




Two-thirds of Ugandan post-colonial life has been under President Museveni. That more Ugandans have been traumatized under his watch than at any time since the 1880s is a legacy his name will be attached to permanently. The first phase of his regime, from 1986 to 2006, was the war era. Crude civil warfare, the conquest phase of his regime, roughly comparable to the first ten years of colonial conquest in its viciousness, characterized Ugandan life. But the Museveni era began, not in 1986, but in 1980, when he started his bush war, after which mass murders and suffering of a kind Uganda had not experienced settled in. 




The end of the Kony war marked the beginning of Museveni’s second phase. But there had been the war, and he was a military ruler. Attempts to govern as a civilian ruler elected in a competitive multiparty system failed and got worse. When at vote count time in 2026, I turned up in my biking gear at my polling station to a gathering of voters with murderous faces (alleging that unknown non-residents were trucked in late to vote) and was confronted by a nasty platoon commander demanding to know what I was doing there, my mind raced to that day in 1987 when Alice Lakwena’s fighters ran past our school, to the news of the 

Mukura train massacre of 1989

, to the elections I had covered beginning in 2001 when, standing at a Gulu polling station, an army truck decanted soldiers who voted without showing cards (I still see soldiers kicking current Justice Minister Nobert Mao in the butt), to 2006 when the real election violence started, and understood one thing: those who harshly judge the Museveni era of militarizing elections are doing him a disservice as well as playing a disingenuous hand. Soldiering is his forte; what else do they expect?




If there was such a thing as Pre-Traumatic Stress Disorder, the country had been quietly absorbing it since the elections of 2006. The culmination of the second Museveni era came with the 2026 elections. Flung now into psychological depths we barely suspected possible, we walk into the future with the unsteady toddling of torture victims learning to walk again. Parts of our lives we once took for granted, such as pragmatic friendliness with a 

boda boda

 rider, now become a nightmare. Is the man only being friendly or is he trying to gain your confidence? Why did he know your house without asking you where you were going? Is the nice waitress a bit too nice? Should you continue eating out? Was that Filipino code number ringing your WhatsApp loading malware? Should you now delete the app? Is it safe to speak from within your own house or should you sit outside to talk?




The aggressive regime of surveillance has become suffocating. I have, not once, not twice, but countless times had to abandon my Facebook account after fake accounts under my name, carrying offensive, erotic images, appeared to my “friends” with only one intention in mind. Thirty years of my journalism, under “David Kaiza”, including my blog, Peoplehouse.blogspot, which carried my reportage of the northern Ugandan war, have all been scrubbed offline. I am not the only Ugandan writer and journalist whose work has disappeared. Each day you navigate ever tighter corridors of your mind, asking if authorial erasure is a prelude to something worse. When they finally come for you, you are a nobody. Like the Revival Movement of the 1930s, the mass of Ugandans turning to spiritualism is staggering. You lie awake at night listening to the desperate prayers; the words “Jesus”, “Mukama” penetrate the walls like jackhammers, or like the demented banging on bulkheads of people trapped in a sinking ship. If you oppose the ruling party, they’ll come for you; worse, if you belong to it, they’ll come for you. The arbitrariness with which the post-Museveni era is building up is breaking Ugandan brains. Is it the beginning of an ethnic pogrom or is this a fight within the first family? And if both are true, then which is not?




The regime of abductions, torture, and forced disappearances had already cratered the foundations of our mental redoubts. But then came the uncovering of the torture regime. The caving in of the mind, when you read through lists of the abducted, the tortured, and the maimed (I shook bodily when I saw the list of pocket contents of colleague Timothy Kalyegira listed in blue ink after his abduction) made you know instinctively that red lines had been crossed, for which retreat was no longer possible. We do not know if we will survive the coming year. The humiliation we feel as Ugandans mounts each time friends from abroad ask you how things are doing. We have not felt this much shame in being Ugandans since the 1970s. But time has not changed: somewhere in a well-funded university, a team of psychology scholars is accumulating literature reviews for a research proposal on Uganda.

Healing the Elephant: Life and History on the Mental Edge of Uganda

 first appeared on 

The Elephant

.

We recently buried our aunt, Wahito. She hailed from Ndumberi in Kiambu County and was my mother’s elder sister. A staunch Catholic, she was practically buried by the Catholic Women Association. Resplendent in their headscarves and their blue and white uniforms, the CWA practically took charge during the long funeral mass. The officiating priest eulogized my aunt, who died at 87, as a beacon of steadfastness in her Catholicism and reminded us that dead men and women tell no tales. She was gone, and we the living had the duty to reclaim our stories. As he wound up his sermon, the priest asked the congregation whether it was steadfast in its resolve to do the right thing come 10 August 2027. The congregation responded in unison, and the 

Wantam

 slogan rent the air. A flash of satisfaction crossed the priest’s face; his smile was unmistakable. At the burial site, the priest was unrelenting: “Once again I implore you, we must do the right thing, and we mustn’t forget.”




The Wantam gospel




The Catholic Church of Kenya, through the powerful voice of Archbishop Anthony Muheria, the Opus Dei cleric overseeing the Nyeri diocese, recently warned its clergy against allowing politics at pulpits across the country. The priest presiding over my aunt’s funeral must have heard Archbishop Muheria loud and clear, but in the Mt Kenya region, the mainstream churches have taken it upon themselves to preach the 

Wantam

 gospel, the clarion call that sums up the opposition to President William Ruto, nine months to the general election. The Church was at the forefront of canvassing for votes for Ruto in the Mt Kenya region in the run-up to the 2022 elections, but less than two years later, after the region had overwhelmingly voted for the president, cracks began to appear, and things were falling apart. 




Christian president




Whatever happened? Why has a community that had overwhelmingly voted for Ruto despite all the iniquities that it accused him of having perpetrated against it now with the same vigour, turned its back on him? In a region that is supremely religious, the mainstream churches – the Anglican Church of Kenya (ACK), the Catholic Church, the Methodist Church, and the Presbyterian Church of East Africa (PCEA) – play a central role in shepherding their congregations in the direction in which it is going to vote. In the lead-up to the August 2022 elections, the churches threw their support behind Ruto and asked their faithful to follow suit. They cast Ruto as a born-again, bible-reading Christian, as opposed to Raila Odinga, whose Christianity was considered dodgy as far as the Mt Kenya region’s religious leaders were concerned. The clerics looked forward to enhanced social engagements with the forthcoming “Christian president”. But woe unto them, because as they would soon find out, President Ruto’s only interest was to capture state power, after which he would discard their “anointed and holy” support.




Betrayal




That betrayal – the feeling of having been used and abused despite the supposedly gentleman’s agreement on an anticipated state – church revival – is what led the Mt Kenya region’s ACK leadership, barely two years into President Ruto’s rule, to ask their congregations for forgiveness for having campaigned for him and for asking them to do the same and vote for him. As an ACK Mt Kenya diocese elder told me, the Church was truly remorseful for having misled its worshippers and regretted its liaison with a president who had deliberately lied to the Church leadership. Always circumspect in its dealings with the state, the leadership of the powerful Catholic Church of Kenya, through the Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops (KCCB), finds President Ruto insincere in his politics – a euphemism for liar. “He lies like a sieve,” one Catholic priest told me. “He believes that the Catholic Church leadership in Mt Kenya is ‘biased’ against him because he’s not a Catholic. The region’s Catholic clergy didn’t fight Mwai Kibaki; why? Because he was a Catholic. The same clergy didn’t fight Uhuru Kenyatta; why? For the same reason; he is Catholic.” Ruto is caught up in his lies and deceptions, and he has come to believe in those lies, said the priest.   




“Ruto lied to us”




If the Church in the Mt Kenya region has experienced betrayal from Ruto, it is the voter who has verbalized that betrayal. As early as 2024, the Mt Kenya region voter complained about the “punitive taxes” that were introduced, especially on the Hass avocado crop that counties like Murang’a are now growing for export mainly to China. The beginning of 2024 saw the government impose a five per cent withholding tax on agricultural produce. For every 100 shillings that the farmers made, the government planned to take 5 shillings. As Ruto crisscrossed the Mt Kenya region campaigning, he spoke of enhancing the region’s agricultural productivity and doing away with unnecessary taxes. The voter was upbeat because he believed Ruto spoke his language of development, as he pretended to understand his socio-economic burden and agriculture-related concerns. Little did the voter know that President Ruto’s focus was on “state capture”. “Ruto lied to us. Once he got into State House, he betrayed the trust we had bestowed on him,” said a voter from Kiambu County. The theme of betrayal is one that has dogged the region since the 

Mau Mau

 insurrection and the State of Emergency in the 1950s. Betrayal is abhorred, and traitors are seen as enemies of the community and people who can never ever be trusted again. “He promised that the 

Mau Mau

 roads project would continue uninterrupted since the money had already been allocated during Uhuru Kenyatta’s tenure. What’s the first thing Ruto did? He stopped their construction,” said the voter from Kiambu County.




Unruly son




By the time the Gen Z protests of June 2024 opposing the Finance Bill were exploding, triggered by the punitive taxes included in the bill, the Mt Kenya region voter had already washed his hands off President Ruto. Four months later, Ruto sealed his fate. Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s 

“unprocedural”

 impeachment in October 2024 was the straw that broke the camel’s back. The impeachment, which was taken by the Mt Kenya voter as having been largely orchestrated by President Ruto himself, confirmed his worst fears: that indeed Ruto didn’t mean well for the region. Granted, then Deputy President Gachagua did not elicit much admiration and love from the region’s voters. Two years into the job, the average voter was ambivalent towards him, was still sizing him up, giving him the benefit of the doubt, but that did not mean he should be tossed around like a tennis ball. Rigathi Gachagua was considered the bridge between the state and the Mt Kenya region. It was an important bridge insofar as the region hoped to keep relations alive. In any case, the region argued that the matter of disciplining Gachagua lay with the voter and not with the state or its appendages. Gachagua may have been unruly, but he still was their son.




Deceitful pose




Naivasha member of parliament Jayne 

Kihara

, a veteran politician who knows President Ruto very well, believes Ruto’s machinations against the Mt Kenya region began as soon as he was elected into office. “The first task we had as the UDA party was to elect East African Legislative Assembly (EALA) MPs,” said Kihara. “We agreed on a formula in the ‘mini-election’ conducted at State House. We had five slots against ODM’s four slots and yet none of the five slots initially went to Mt Kenya, a region that had propelled Ruto to the presidency. When we as Mt Kenya MPs asked what was going on, the retort from President Ruto’s [Kalenjin] camp was, ‘But what did you want?’ I’ve worked with Ruto for many years, but it was not until he became president that I came to now fully understand him,” said Kihara. “He had always hidden his deceitful pose towards the Kikuyu, but once he became president, he couldn’t hide it any longer,” Kihara says the EALA debacle was the clearest first sign that Ruto was hellbent on betraying the Mt Kenya region. “Can you imagine, he would stop us from caucusing as Mt Kenya region’s MPs, terming such caucuses tribal, while all the time, the other UDA MPs from their respective ethnic regions caucused freely.”




Trooping to DCP




Unhappy with the Finance Bill 2024, the Mt Kenya voter escalated his anger to include all the Kenya region MPs who had voted for it. Today, the Mt Kenya region voter has a list of all the MPs who voted for the bill and who are to be punished alongside Ruto in August 2027. Gen Zs too have their list of the 60 comrades who were killed during the protests. They may not currently know who they will vote for, but they know who they will vote against: President Ruto and all the MPs who voted for the Finance Bill 2024. Unable to continue pretending they can contain the heat of rejection, some of the Mt Kenya UDA MPs have started trooping to the Gachagua-led party – the Democracy for Citizens Party (DCP). They have been given a clear warning, however: the electorate will be waiting for you; they are the final arbiter, says the impeached former deputy president.




No respite




If President Ruto hopes for respite from the Mt Kenya region’s churches that wholly supported him in 2022, he is in for a rude shock. The PCEA Church leadership was so angry with the Mwiki PCEA church attack on 6 April 2025 that its leadership refused to meet him at State House, Nairobi. To save face, State House mandarins have been spinning the matter of the visit as coming from the PCEA itself and not as an invitation from State House. After Gachagua’s impeachment was ratified by the Senate on 17 October 2024, his public appearances were henceforth dogged by chaos and rowdy mobs that interrupted his meetings. His first post-impeachment meeting was at Bibirioni, in Limuru constituency, on 28 November 2024, where he attended the burial of a young man, Erastus Nduati. The violence meted out on the mourners and the destruction of vehicles and plastic seats was so well choreographed that it was obvious that the hooligans, armed with crude weapons that included iron bars and paramilitary General Service Unit (GSU)-type batons, had free rein to cause chaos and inflict bodily harm on those present. Gachagua’s vehicle was pelted with rocks and “beaten” with batons as his security team whisked him away from the mayhem. In all probability, the bedlam was directed at him, and everybody else was merely collateral damage. The Bibirioni violence seems to have just been the beginning of the unmitigated chaos that would follow him wherever he had a public engagement, which was mostly in churches.        




Bitter memories




But the January 2026 attack at the ACK Church in Witima, Othaya Constituency, Nyeri County, was for the church leadership the tipping point, the point of rupture with President Ruto’s regime. The ACK elder said that the desecration of the Witima church, where worshippers, including children and their mothers, were frighteningly exposed to unwarranted violence, proved that President Ruto had declared war on the community and there was no turning back on his rejection by the Mt Kenya region electorate. “We cannot wait for August to vote Ruto out, and that is what we have been preaching to our congregation.” Gachagua was at the church, but no sooner had he settled down than police tear gas canisters were lobbed into the church, presumably by police in civilian clothing, or by assailants trained on how to lob tear gas. Once again, the former DP’s security team had to hurdle around him and create an escape route. 




These two particular attacks, perpetrated within church precincts, places which, whatever you may think, are still considered sacred sanctuaries, have evoked bitter memories of the burning of the Kiambaa church, in Burnt Forest, Uasin Gishu County, in the North Rift. The wooden Pentecostal church was the ugly site of the post-election violence of 2007–2008 that targeted ethnic Kikuyu residing in Kalenjin land. Today, in the Mt Kenya region, the Kikuyu from Central Kenya in particular, berate themselves for campaigning and voting for Ruto. “It is as if we’d been jinxed. How is it that we voted for a person who allegedly has been associated with the killings of our people in North Rift? It was a big mistake on our part to presume forgiveness and to allow ourselves to be duped by sweetened political lies, fake tears and emotional blackmail.”




Stereotypes




After Gachagua was deposed, the voter was told that within two weeks Gachagua would be forgotten and, in case the voter didn’t forget about the impeachment within 14 days, he would be bribed with money, because anyway, the Mt Kenya voter loves money like a harlot. It is an insult that dug deep, especially among the baby boomer generation, an anger that the voter had been incubating and which found expression on 16 July 2026, the day of the Ol Kalou by-election. President Ruto and his acolytes had poured hundreds of millions of shillings into the constituency, in the hope that the cash handouts would sway the voter’s resolve. Voters were induced with MPesa cash transfers, receiving 5,000 shillings early in the morning as an incentive to vote for the UDA candidate. “We wanted to prove to Ruto that money doesn’t define us – poverty or otherwise. To refer to us in those very derogatory and demeaning terms was deeply hurtful and the ultimate insult,” said a voter from Ol Kalou. “We proved our point, as indeed we will in August 2027.”




The victory of DCP candidate Sammy Douglas Kamau Waweru in the by-election was therefore a whitewash of the ruling party’s candidate, Samuel Muchina Nyagah: 35,000 votes to 5,000, a ratio of 7:1. The UDA drubbing by Gachagua’s DCP, a party which is slightly over a year old – it was formed in May 2025 – threw UDA hawks into a frenzy of anger, bitterness, and sheer callousness. A few days later, Cabinet Secretary for Health Aden Duale, speaking in his native tongue in Lafey constituency in Mandera County, likened the Kikuyu community to the proverbial hyena. The fables taught to us about the hyena described it as ugly, greedy, and a scavenger. Put on the spot over the remark, in typical Kenyan politician’s style, Duale said that he had been misquoted. Unremorseful, Duale refused to apologize, and with his unfortunate remarks, he hardened Kikuyus’ resolve to vote out Ruto and his representatives in the Mt Kenya region.




The position of the Catholic priest who presided over my aunt’s burial is increasingly becoming the norm in the Mt Kenya region, where the clergy has taken it upon itself to preach the 

Wantam

 gospel in churches and at social occasions such as funerals, weddings, and dowry ceremonies.

How Ruto Lost Gikuyus and What Happens Next?

content:

Its story is inseparable from Kenya’s own: the making of a nation, the defence of a public sphere, and now the struggle to preserve that public sphere in a digital, politically pressured age. 




From Taifa to Nation

Taifa

title: The Decline of The Nation: From Taifa to Taarifa
content:
When I worked at the Nation Media Group (NMG), there was a running joke about the immortality of 

Taifa Leo

, the Swahili newspaper printed by the media group that 20-year-old Prince Karim had bought in 1959 when he became the Fourth Aga Khan.




From this £10,000 purchase from British officer and former District Commissioner Charles Hayes, the group would grow to control the largest circulation of newspapers, and television stations and websites across East Africa.




Over time, the Swahili paper did face dwindling audiences as demographic changes produced a more cosmopolitan youth who found reading news in grammatical Swahili a hard sell and was more inclined to consume short video content online. 




Despite this handicap, 

Taifa Leo

 owes its longevity to the sentimental connection to its founder, His Highness the Aga Khan. For its survival, it also relied on punchy yet witty headlines, humorous angles, and 

Bi Taifa

, a cover model featured on one of its pages that was primarily produced by Taifa Leo photographers. If you hung around these photographers long enough, you would get to see how the allure of appearing on the tabloid would create new customers looking out for their photos. 




Then the Fourth Aga Khan died, and 

Taifa Leo

’s business model was finally facing the test of succession, a shift in the media landscape, and an uncertain future under Tanzanian billionaire Rostam Aziz who may share the paper’s Swahili heritage but not the paper’s founding ideals that had inspired its punchy headlines. 




Succession




The Fourth Aga Khan’s strategy with 

Taifa Leo

 was to create a sustainable, independent, and influential media platform that would inform the public and strengthen the fabric of the newly independent nation.




A younger Aga Khan had borne the cost of the loss-making venture in its first decade and had 

fought off attempts

 by the family of Kenya’s first president, Jomo Kenyatta, to gain control of the media house and turn it into an organ of state propaganda. 




But as the Aga Khan grew older and gradually relinquished his stake to other shareholders and to a professional board, this legacy of defending the sanctity of media freedom began to wane. 




Under the younger Kenyatta, the old Aga Khan’s legacy project 

gave in to state interference

 in what could be linked to privileges and immunities granted to the Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN) and its affiliated agencies, which were classified as philanthropic, charitable and non-profit-making.




But even tax exemptions and the economies of scale of running Aga Khan’s conglomerates across East Africa could not save the businesses’ fortunes and their decline in profitability would lead to divestments under his son, Prince Rahim Al-Hussaini, the Fifth Aga Khan, shortly after the patriarch’s death.




Shifting landscapes




I owe a huge part of my journalism career to the late Prince Karim Aga Khan, having worked at Nation Media Group where I learned the trade until I transitioned into private practice a couple of years ago.




But even as I transitioned out, I was still a beneficiary of his benevolence when I enlisted for a course titled “Beyond the Newsroom” that aimed to help journalists move on following the job cuts that had become the norm in the industry.




This programme demonstrated that the Aga Khan understood the dynamics of our evolving media industry and had chosen to help incubate future media start-ups through the Aga Khan University Graduate School of Media and Communications.




I found myself sitting in a lecture hall where two of the trainers now teaching journalists how to cope beyond the newsroom had been the managers who had hired me into the profession.




David Aduda had hired me at the Nation Media Group in 2013, then three years later, Joseph Odindo poached me to join Standard Media Group. But they were now both with the Aga Khan University School of Media, providing sponsored training to the scores of journalists made redundant by the decline of traditional media.




Golden age




I muscled my way into journalism as a fresh graduate from Maseno University, moving to the capital and into a profession that was brimming with opportunity.




In 2013, Kenya was undergoing a rather calm political transition and the world had forgotten about the financial crisis. Anything seemed possible, including printing money.




I first interned at the NMG when it was making KSh13.3 billion in revenues and netting KSh2.5 billion in profits. You can imagine my surprise when, after undergoing intense interviews, psychometric tests, and questions about quantitative easing (the new name of printing money), I was handed a KSh7,000 contract.




But I believed in the calling. I remember visiting the Kenya Television Network as a member of the Debate and Journalism club while in high school, and the Nation Centre when I was a university student, and telling myself that one day I would work where once Whispers had worked; he fascinated me when I was young. I lived in a derelict building somewhere in Kariobangi where the rent was KSh5,000, but I still signed on the dotted line and then convinced my father and my sister to underwrite the risk.




It paid off; I walked into a vibrant newsroom and got to meet and work with Ken Walibora. I sat in that part of the newsroom known as “Migingo”, the desks nearest those of Ugandans Onyango Obbo and Daniel Kalinaki. Back then the newsroom was so vibrant it scouted universities for the best talent to bring into its media lab programme – writers like Jacqueline Kubania, Cornell Ngare, and Waga Odongo.




Decline




I tell anyone who cares to listen that I have witnessed the industry transform. At the time, we interns were not assigned computers, so we would hang around, sitting on the chairs meant for the group’s drivers, waiting for “Mayor of Migingo” John Ngirachu to leave for parliament, or for some other senior journalist to go for an assignment, and pounce on their desks to write those little briefs whose authorship no one knew.




But by the time I left the newsroom, I was surrounded by four empty desks; I could have written an introduction at one and concluded my story at another of those unused workstations where once such and such a colleague used to sit. Where are they now? 




I met some of them while attending the Beyond the Newsroom training; right in front of me on the very first day were Aduda and Odindo. They had transitioned themselves and were now passing on their wealth of experience to us.




I had attended Odindo’s leaving party and had felt at the time that this was what media success looked like; the charming speeches celebrated him, and he seemed almost agreeable to what was an inevitable goodbye.




Business convergence, digital reorganizations




Since then journalists have not been given such lavish send-offs. Their departures have instead been announced by internal memo or through the regular cycles of redundancies, business convergence, and all manner of digital reorganizations. Exits have become a source of industry anxiety; the despair, the uncertainty and the anger at having loved a dog’s life and being rejected via a cursory letter, a phone call, a disabled email address, or a cancelled entry pass.




It turns out Odindo took it just as hard as the rest of us when we left the newsroom. He made a short return to the industry at the 

Standard

 before joining the Aga Khan Media School as a trainer. Through it all, the lesson for the veteran had been to remember who he really was – a good editor who did his work diligently, managing other editors and overseeing a newsroom over the years – and therein lay his strength.




And as he sought himself in the shock therapy that is retirement, digging through piles of old documents, the words of a distant headmaster on his report card saying, “Joseph is capable of much more” lent him the courage to try new things.




But tell that to a pack of depressed former journalists thrown into the tailspin of sudden joblessness – the struggle to pay rent and school fees, learning to take rejection from job applications, being worried sick about lacking insurance and, above all, losing the power and privileges that come with working for a huge news organization. Journalism is a strange profession, built around the façade of the glamorous television anchors, powerful owners, backed by human rights defenders and international patronage. But once you step off, the entire network freezes you out.




But even in the midst of this despair, a group of journalists attending the training found solace in each other’s company, sharing their experiences, their unvoiced emotions. As we shared our stories and learned the limitations of our mindsets to our present careers, the opportunities available to our skill sets and, really thinking about our industry, it became apparent why the Aga Khan’s initiative to help transition the industry was so important.




Structured monopoly




Prince Karim Aga Khan, who grew up in Nairobi and founded the 

Daily Nation

 in the 1960s, has for decades underwritten media freedom and its success in Kenya, using his financial muscle to shoulder the capital-intensive business and leveraging its power to support his massive business ventures in hospitality, energy, agriculture, insurance, and finance. 




The newspaper model had, over the years, become archaic, relying on central printing and physical distribution through an expensive logistical network. This costly structure acted as an entry barrier, making the industry a near monopoly for those who could afford to own it.




The internet completely disrupted this distribution model, replacing the newspaper with a mobile telephone and a computer screen that virtually made anyone with an internet connection a potential journalist. This happened at a time when America was printing money through quantitative easing, which was funnelled to tech companies to finance experiments on customer targeting. The social media model that allowed companies to study the individual and influence their behaviour changed how advertising was done and the role of the media as gatekeeper of audiences. Social media ate legacy media’s lunch, and as advertising revenues dropped, the cost of maintaining media operations became increasingly high. Media houses reacted by cutting costs and trimming staff numbers.




The Nation Group’s profits have been in sharp decline, falling from KSh2.5 billion when I joined the company in 2013 to a loss of KSh308.6 million in 2025. In the same period, the group’s staff nearly halved – from 1,980 to 

1,100

 – due to the annual ritual of rationalization that has only served to heighten anxiety in the newsroom.




“We were too busy doing the traditional thing. We knew about the disruptions from technology but were engrossed in the product to make money for the employer that we ignored digital. We were so engrossed in competition for the little space doing what we had done for so long,” Odindo told us during the training.




Now digital is viewed as the magic bullet even though newsrooms know that the same technology is spelling their end. 




“Notwithstanding the operating performance for the period, the gains recorded in digital and broadcasting underscore the Group’s sustained pivot toward a scalable digital business and optimization of the growth headroom in broadcasting. Therefore, the Group continues to invest in unified technology to enhance customer experience across our platforms, diversify audience demographics and accelerate monetization of our expansive digital assets,” the 

Nation

’s board of directors said in its 2025 results outlook.




Business interests 




It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. As the media business shrank, so did the interest of its benevolent founder. 




Even as the newspaper model began to collapse, the Aga Khan’s interests shifted elsewhere – to his multiple businesses that include the Aga Khan Hospital, the TPS Serena hotel chain, Jubilee Insurers and Diamond Trust Bank, IPSK and Farmers Choice, and power stations. He sought to secure tax concessions for them at the expense of media independence. 




Inevitably, politicians took advantage of the dire straits in which the media found itself, using advertising revenues to leverage friendly coverage. The government weaponized media revenues, using its power as the largest advertiser to accumulate invoices that crippled the newsrooms and then withholding advertising altogether before negotiating the cost of advertising downwards by having the leading newspapers carry the government’s 

MyGov

 pamphlet as an insert.




As the handshake extended beyond the elbow, so did the pressure to push out dissenting journalists like Dennis Galava and Godfrey Mwampembwa (Gaddo), which gave the Aga Khan a bad press for what was seen as giving in to the demands of a government averse to criticism. 




Like the Children of Gebelawi, we wondered what the Aga Khan thought as he watched the empire that he had built over decades go into decline.




Last man standing




After President Daniel Moi left office, fortunes at the 

Standard

 were not good either. Between 2024 and 2015, the firm only made profits twice in a decade as the losses widened to over a billion in the last years (KSh1.1 billion in 2024). In newsrooms, the Standard Group’s losses were glossed over while the company struggled to pay correspondents – contract writers who are paid by the length of each published article. The silence continued even as the late payment of salaries finally hit permanent staff and the industry slid slowly into the practice of not paying journalists on time and sometimes not at all.




The 

Standard

 newspaper blamed its troubles on the state’s non-payment of outstanding bills despite the fact that its owner, Gideon Moi, was part of President Uhuru Kenyatta’s inner circle in Azimio.




Despite the dip in fortunes, the paper has maintained its relevance through bold headlines critical of President William Ruto’s regime to recover falling circulation. The newspaper gives Gideon Moi leverage in shaping public opinion. He is reported to have 

turned down

 an offer from Ruto’s allies who had been seeking to acquire a stake in the struggling Standard Group.




According to Africa Intelligence, President Ruto then turned his 

sights on NMG

, having bagged 

The Star

 to start building a media empire through which to control the narrative ahead of the 2027 presidential election.




With the Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development agreeing to sell its entire 

shareholding in NPRT Holdings Africa Limited

 to Taarifa Limited, which is owned by Tanzanian Business Magnate Rostam Aziz, many see this as the takeover of East Africa’s most powerful media house by politically linked patronage. It is expected that Aziz’s business and political interests will either rapidly reshape the editorial line or cull the paper’s ranks much in the manner that Jeff Bezos did at the 

Washington Post.




Nation Media Group has already reorganized its board of directors and shaken the editorial team, pushing out senior editors to subsidiaries across the region and replacing them with acting managers. With rumours of incoming fresh blood to replace some of the senior team members, those in acting roles will be under pressure to be more pliable in fronting the state’s narratives.




Owning the public square




Traditionally, Kenyan newsrooms have suffered rifts among editors as elections draw closer. But when the newsrooms were full, you could mediate interests because no one could capture all the editors, and both sides of the story got to be told. But as the job cuts did away with the fat flesh and came close to the bone, the newsroom grew smaller and became easier and cheaper to capture. 




The editors who should have seen this coming were busy fighting each other in a battle for survival. Editors conspired to push each other out in a game of musical chairs that made it a slippery climb to the top deck. 




With fewer and fewer journalists to deal with, the political class was better able to manage the media. Politicians also saw an opportunity to turn prominent media voices that used to keep them in check into tools for propaganda. They are now hiring scores of former journalists to sing their praises as they further weaken the fourth estate.




I believe that journalists still have a chance to save the profession if we can see our demise and organize quickly to build alternatives. The industry needs a large enough shared space that can safeguard media independence, underwrite the security of journalists, and leverage having several journalists offering a range of public opinion that is not controlled by large corporates or politicians.  




In the end, storytelling is immortal notwithstanding the channels and models through which it is delivered through time.
